newsitem.title: USA: IMF says Kenya will lose loan unless govt acts soon.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Kenya will lose loan unless govt acts soon.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund, warning Kenya to make its much-criticised public sector more transparent and accountable, said on Thursday that a big IMF loan would lapse unless Nairobi acted within a week.
An IMF spokesman said a mission had visited Kenya this month, but that measures taken by the government since a previous IMF warning had fallen short of expectations.
"Under the circumstances the current annual (loan) arrangement will be allowed to lapse on July 1," he said.

The IMF extended Kenya a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment loan worth a total of $205 million in April last year, but regular payments were conditional on Kenya meeting its promises on reform issues.

The last scheduled payment, a $36 million tranche, was delayed by the IMF for a month June 30, partly because of concern about the way the Kenyan authorities had handled a multimillion-dollar financial scandal.

"The inability of the government to make use of several extensions of the first annual ESAF arrangement and take decisive steps to ensure transparency and accountability in the use of public funds and resolve outstanding energy sector reform issues has a direct bearing on the prospects for attaining the objectives of the ESAF support programme," the IMF spokesman said.

Offering a glimmer of hope to the authorities in Nairobi, he added: "It could still be possible to complete the review of the ESAF if the Kenyan government were to take strong measures within the next week."

This would include efforts to strengthen the economic management of the energy sector and firm government commitments to act in other areas "particularly establishing accountability in relation to regular budgetary payments."

The debate about the release of the IMF loan comes amid clashes in Kenyan cities between government forces and groups demanding constitutional reform that want to reduce the powers of President Daniel arap Moi.

IMF officials said earlier this month that the IMF wanted the government to clarify what it planned to do to counter "irregularities" that made a big financial scandal possible. They were asking what the government would do to recover lost money.

The scandal involves Goldenberg International, a firm that was paid millions of dollars under an export compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces little gold and has no diamond deposits.
